461.event_title: Disraeli buys Egypt's Suez Canal shares for Britain
461.event: When Egypt's ruler Isma'il Pasha, deep in debt, put up for sale his country's shares in the Suez Canal Company, nearly half of all its shares, the British government under Benjamin Disraeli bought them for about four million pounds. The Foreign Office had advised against the purchase, and because Parliament was not sitting, Disraeli obtained the money as a loan from the banking house of N. M. Rothschild and Sons, which the government repaid within months.
461.explanation: A large immediate outlay bought Britain a major stake in the shortest sea route to India, a gain that shaped its policy in the region for decades.
461.tie_back: The kural asks a ruler to set what will be spent against what will be gained and the yield that follows, and Disraeli's purchase was a case of paying a heavy price now for a lasting strategic return.
461._accuracy_note: A real case of outlay weighed against long-term gain, but the sources stress the speed of the decision more than any careful three-part reckoning of the kind the kural describes.

462.event_title: The Delta Committee plans the Netherlands' Delta Works
462.event: After the North Sea flood of 1 February 1953 killed more than 1,800 people in the Netherlands, the government set up a Delta Committee of experts led by the director-general of Rijkswaterstaat, A. G. Maris, within weeks. Its studies produced the Delta Plan in 1955, which became law in 1958, and over the following decades engineers built a chain of dams, sluices and storm-surge barriers, ending with the Eastern Scheldt barrier in 1986.
462.explanation: A task once thought impossible, closing off the sea arms of the southwestern delta while keeping key shipping routes open, was achieved through years of study by a chosen body of specialists.
462.tie_back: The kural promises that nothing is too hard for those who deliberate with well-chosen counsellors and examine matters themselves, and the Delta Works grew from exactly such a committee.
462._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of chosen experts deliberating before a vast undertaking; the kural's stress on personal examination by the leader is less visible.

463.event_title: Long-Term Capital Management's leveraged bets collapse
463.event: The hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management earned thin margins on each trade and borrowed heavily to magnify them, holding about 30 dollars of debt for every dollar of its own capital by the end of 1997. After Russia's debt default in August 1998 set off market turmoil, the fund lost 44 percent of its value in that month alone. In September the Federal Reserve Bank of New York brought together fourteen banks and brokerages, which put about 3.6 billion dollars into the fund so that its holdings could be wound down in an orderly way.
463.explanation: The fund's pursuit of extra profit through borrowing put its own capital, and that of its lenders, at risk, and the losses came far faster than the gains had.
463.tie_back: The kural says the wise will not chase future profit by risking the capital they already hold, which is exactly the risk that heavy borrowing created for this fund.
463._accuracy_note: Very close to the kural's commercial image of staking the principal for hoped-for gain, though the actors were investment managers rather than a ruler.

464.event_title: The warship Vasa sinks on her maiden voyage
464.event: A few weeks before the Swedish royal warship Vasa sailed, Admiral Klas Fleming had thirty men run back and forth across her deck to test her stability, and onlookers could see that she failed the test. The ship sailed anyway, and within minutes of setting out on her first voyage a gust of wind heeled her over, water poured in through the open lower gunports, and she sank in Stockholm harbour in front of a large crowd. Around 30 of those on board died, and the wreck was raised in 1961 and is now displayed in the Vasa Museum.
464.explanation: The most powerful warship in the Baltic became a public humiliation for the Swedish crown because doubts about whether she could sail safely were never resolved before she set out.
464.tie_back: The kural warns that those who fear disgrace do not begin a venture whose outcome is unclear, and the Vasa sailed with exactly such an unresolved doubt and ended in public disgrace.
464._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation: a known uncertainty, a venture begun anyway, and a public humiliation witnessed by the whole city.

465.event_title: The Jameson Raid into the Transvaal
465.event: Leander Starr Jameson led about 500 armed men from the borders of Bechuanaland into the Boer republic of the Transvaal, expecting a rising by foreign residents in Johannesburg that never happened. The column was surrounded and surrendered at Doornkop on 2 January 1896. Cecil Rhodes was forced to resign as prime minister of the Cape Colony, while President Paul Kruger gained international sympathy and won re-election in 1896.
465.explanation: The badly prepared raid did not weaken Kruger's government but made it stronger and deepened the divisions that led to the South African War of 1899-1902.
465.tie_back: The kural says an attack launched without thorough planning settles the enemy in a prepared bed where he grows strong, and the Jameson Raid left Kruger more secure than before.
465._accuracy_note: Close to a dramatisation of the kural's image: a hasty, poorly planned assault that strengthened the very opponent it targeted.

466.event_title: The Quebec Bridge collapses during construction
466.event: The design of the Quebec Bridge's long cantilever span had been enlarged, but its dead load had been calculated using weights for the original, shorter span. In August 1907 the inspector Norman McLure reported that key compression members were bending and the bend was growing, yet the chief engineer insisted that work continue; McLure's urgent advice that no more load be placed on the bridge was relayed only on 27 August, and the south arm collapsed two days later, killing 75 workers. A royal commission found that faulty design and inadequate engineering supervision had caused the disaster.
466.explanation: The failure came both from what was done wrongly, a miscalculated design, and from what was left undone, halting the work when the warnings appeared.
466.tie_back: The kural says ruin comes both from doing what should not be done and from failing to do what should be done, and the Quebec Bridge failed through both kinds of error at once.
466._accuracy_note: A clear case of commission and omission combining in one documented failure, though the kural speaks in more general moral terms.

467.event_title: Construction of the Sydney Opera House begins before the design is resolved
467.event: Work on the Sydney Opera House began in 1959, pressed forward before a state election, long before Jorn Utzon's design for the roof shells and their supports had been worked out. As each new design was produced the cost rose and the completion date moved back, and the estimated cost of 3.5 million pounds had reached 13.7 million by 1962. After a dispute with the state government over payments, Utzon resigned in 1966, and other architects completed the building, which opened in 1973.
467.explanation: The building became a world icon, but starting before the plan was settled led to years of delay, a vastly higher cost and the departure of its architect.
467.tie_back: The kural calls it a disgrace to say we will think it through after we have begun, and the Opera House was begun on precisely that basis.
467._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of beginning first and deliberating afterwards, with the documented costs that followed.

468.event_title: The French attempt to build the Panama Canal fails
468.place: Isthmus of Panama (then part of Colombia)
468.event: Ferdinand de Lesseps, celebrated for building the Suez Canal, led a French company that began digging a sea-level canal across Panama in 1881, financed by public share subscriptions in France. Landslides, flooding and tropical diseases defeated the method, and an estimated 22,000 workers died; a change to a lock canal came only in 1887. In 1889 the shareholders dissolved the company and all work stopped, with about 40 percent of the excavation done.
468.explanation: Great prestige, huge sums of money and the backing of many investors could not save a plan built on a method that did not suit the ground.
468.tie_back: The kural says effort not spent in the proper way will fail even if many stand by to support it, and the French canal collapsed despite vast public backing because its method was wrong.
468._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of wide support failing to rescue an unsuitable method, which is the kural's precise point.

469.event_title: The Macartney Embassy's gifts fail to impress the Qianlong Emperor
469.event: Britain sent Lord George Macartney to the Qing court with a large retinue and a great quantity of presents, including clocks, carriages and scientific instruments, hoping to open more ports and station an ambassador in China. The Qianlong Emperor treated the presents as tribute and, in edicts addressed to King George III, rejected every British request, stating that China had no need of Britain's manufactures.
469.explanation: Lavish gifts chosen without understanding how the recipient's court saw the world produced the opposite of the intended effect.
469.tie_back: The kural warns that even well-meant giving can fail when one does not understand the nature of the person receiving it, and Britain's gifts misjudged the emperor and his court.
469._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the gifts did fail through misreading the recipient, but the embassy was a trade mission rather than an act of pure benevolence.

470.event_title: Emperor Nero competes at the Olympic Games
470.event: During a tour of Greece, the Roman emperor Nero competed in the Greek games, adding contests in music and tragedy to the Olympic programme. At Olympia he drove a ten-horse chariot, fell from it and did not finish the race, yet was proclaimed the winner.
470.explanation: An emperor performing as a competitor and accepting a victory he had not earned became a lasting example of conduct unworthy of a ruler.
470.tie_back: The kural says the world will not approve what does not suit one's own station, and Nero's games turned his rank into an object of ridicule.
470._accuracy_note: A strong example of an act unbefitting one's position, though the ancient accounts of Nero come from writers already hostile to him.
